boards.prompt: Draw an I-section and get its second moment of area. Which part carries the bending moment and which part carries the shear? Now estimate the web shear stress quickly.
points: Parallel axis theorem: I = Σ(I_c + A d²), and the flange A d² terms dominate
Thin flanges: I ≈ 2 b t_f (h/2)² + t_w h³/12
The flanges carry most of the bending moment as a tension and compression couple
The web carries most of the shear force
Web shear stress is nearly uniform, so τ ≈ V/(h t_w) is a good quick estimate

boards.prompt: Derive the shear stress distribution in a solid rectangular beam under shear V. Where is it largest and how large? Now do a solid circle.
points: Longitudinal equilibrium of a cut slice gives τ = VQ/(Ib)
Q is the first moment of the area beyond the cut about the neutral axis
Rectangle: τ = (6V/(bh³))(h²/4 − y²), a parabola
τ is zero at the top and bottom free surfaces and largest at the neutral axis
Rectangle peak τ_max = 3V/(2A); solid circle peak τ_max = 4V/(3A)

boards.prompt: Keep loading a rectangular steel beam in bending past first yield. Sketch the stress through the depth as it goes, and give me the shape factor. Is an I-beam's shape factor higher or lower?
points: First yield at the extreme fibre: M_y = σ_y bh²/6
An elastic core shrinks while the outer zones sit at σ_y (elastic perfectly plastic)
Fully plastic: M_p = σ_y bh²/4, forming a plastic hinge
Shape factor M_p/M_y = 1.5 for a rectangle
An I-beam has a lower shape factor, about 1.1 to 1.2, since its flanges are already near yield at first yield

boards.prompt: Integrate the beam equation for a cantilever with a tip load and get the tip deflection and slope. Now add a uniform load on top: how do you get the combined deflection fast?
points: Moment-curvature: EI w″ = M(x)
Clamped root: w(0) = 0 and w′(0) = 0 fix the integration constants
Tip load P: δ = PL³/(3EI) and tip slope PL²/(2EI)
Uniform load w: δ = wL⁴/(8EI)
Linear elasticity and small deflections allow superposition, so the deflections add

boards.prompt: Find the shear center of a thin open semicircular section of radius R and thickness t under a vertical shear V.
points: Start the shear flow at zero at a free edge and use q = VQ/I
I = πR³t/2 about the horizontal axis through the centre
Q = tR² sin θ, so q = 2V sin θ/(πR), peaking at the neutral axis
Moment of q about the centre: ∫ q R² dθ = 4VR/π
Shear center at e = 4R/π from the centre, beyond the wall since 4/π > 1

boards.prompt: Build in one end of a thin open I-beam and twist the other. Why is it stiffer than Saint-Venant torsion predicts, and what stresses appear at the wall?
points: Open sections warp freely under Saint-Venant torsion, with T = GJθ′
A built-in end restrains warping, which induces axial normal stresses in the flanges
The flanges bend in their own planes in opposite directions, and their shear forces form an extra torque
Total torque T = GJθ′ − EΓθ‴, with Γ the warping constant
The restraint effect decays over a length √(EΓ/(GJ)) from the wall

boards.prompt: Idealize a wing box as booms carrying direct stress and thin skins carrying shear only. Find the shear flows under a vertical shear.
points: Booms carry all the direct stress; skins carry constant shear flow between booms
I = Σ B_r y_r² over the booms
Crossing boom r, the shear flow changes by (V/I) B_r y_r
Cut the closed cell, build the open flows, then add q₀
q₀ comes from moment equivalence of the shear flows with the applied shear

boards.prompt: A thin closed single-cell tube has walls of different thickness and carries a torque T. Where is the shear stress largest and what is the twist rate?
points: Bredt: shear flow q = T/(2A) is constant around the cell
A is the area enclosed by the wall midline
τ = q/t, so the peak shear stress is in the thinnest wall
Twist rate θ′ = (T/(4A²G))∮ ds/t
Torsion constant J = 4A²/∮ ds/t, set mostly by the long thin walls

boards.prompt: Find the vertical deflection of a loaded joint in a pin-jointed truss with an energy method.
points: Find real member forces N from statics
Apply a unit load at the joint along the wanted displacement and find member forces n
Unit load (virtual work): δ = Σ N n L/(EA)
Members carry axial force only, so only axial strain energy enters
A positive result means the joint moves in the unit load direction

boards.prompt: Contrast the principle of minimum total potential energy with minimum total complementary energy. What does each enforce and where does Castigliano fit?
points: Total potential Π = U − W is stationary over kinematically admissible displacements and gives equilibrium
Total complementary Π* = U* − Σ R Δ̄ is stationary over statically admissible forces and gives compatibility
Castigliano's first theorem: P = ∂U/∂Δ
Castigliano's second theorem: Δ = ∂U*/∂P, equal to ∂U/∂P for linear elasticity
Assumed displacement (Ritz) solutions are too stiff; assumed force solutions are too flexible

boards.prompt: Write the strain energy of a member carrying axial force, bending, torsion and shear. For a slender beam, which term dominates and by how much?
points: U = ∫ [N²/(2EA) + M²/(2EI) + T²/(2GJ) + αV²/(2GA)] dx
α is the shear correction factor, 6/5 for a rectangle
Bending dominates for slender beams
Shear deflection relative to bending deflection scales as (h/L)²
Axial energy dominates in pin-jointed trusses

boards.prompt: Use one sine term in Ritz for a simply supported beam under a uniform load q. How close is the midspan deflection, and which way is it off?
points: w = a sin(πx/L) satisfies the kinematic conditions w(0) = w(L) = 0
Π = (EIπ⁴/(4L³))a² − 2qLa/π
∂Π/∂a = 0 gives a = 4qL⁴/(π⁵EI) ≈ 0.01307 qL⁴/EI
Exact midspan deflection is 5qL⁴/(384EI) ≈ 0.01302 qL⁴/EI, so one term lands within 0.4%
Ritz underestimates the work-conjugate quantity ∫ q w dx; a pointwise value can sit on either side, here slightly above

boards.prompt: Here is a shallow two-bar truss with a vertical load at the apex. Sketch load against apex deflection and tell me what happens at the peak.
points: The path rises to a load maximum where dP/dw = 0: a limit point
At the limit point the structure snaps through dynamically to the inverted configuration
The branch between the two limit points is unstable
Displacement control can trace the falling branch
This is a limit point instability, distinct from bifurcation, as in shallow arches and domes

boards.prompt: Π(θ) = ½Cθ² − PL(1 − cos θ) for a rigid bar with a base spring. At P = C/L the second derivative vanishes. Is that equilibrium stable? Now repeat for the bar with a horizontal top spring.
points: Zero second derivative makes the second-order test inconclusive
Go to higher derivatives in order: the first nonzero one decides
The third derivative vanishes by symmetry, so the fourth decides
Base spring: quartic coefficient +PLθ⁴/24 is positive, so the critical point is stable
Horizontal spring: quartic coefficient −kL²θ⁴/8 at P = kL is negative, so the critical point is unstable

boards.prompt: For an n-degree-of-freedom conservative system, how do you get every critical load and mode from the Hessian? What if two critical loads coincide?
points: Linearized second variation: Hessian K − P K_G, stiffness minus load geometric matrix
det(K − P K_G) = 0 is a generalized eigenvalue problem
Eigenvalues are critical loads and eigenvectors are mode shapes
The lowest eigenvalue is the physical P_cr reached on increasing load
Coincident critical loads give compound branching with mode interaction and stronger imperfection sensitivity

boards.prompt: Compare post-buckling of a pinned column, a simply supported plate and an axially compressed thin cylinder.
points: Column (elastica): stable symmetric but nearly flat, P/P_E ≈ 1 + θ₀²/8 with θ₀ the end slope
Plate: stable symmetric with a large post-buckling reserve from membrane stretching (effective width)
Cylinder: unstable symmetric and highly imperfection sensitive
Cylinder test loads fall well below the classical value, so design uses knockdown factors
The post-buckling curvature sets imperfection sensitivity

boards.prompt: Count the degree of static indeterminacy for a propped cantilever, a two-bay continuous beam, a closed rectangular frame and a truss. Give me the rules.
points: Plane beams and frames: external degree = reactions − 3
Each closed loop adds 3 internal redundants
Each internal hinge releases one
Plane trusses: degree = m + r − 2j
A negative degree means a mechanism; a positive degree counts the redundants

boards.prompt: Three bars meet at one joint: a vertical middle bar of length L and two outer bars at angle β to it, all with the same EA. A vertical load P hangs from the joint. Find the bar forces.
points: Symmetry leaves two unknown forces and one equilibrium equation: N₁ + 2N₂ cos β = P
Compatibility: outer bar elongation equals δ cos β, with outer length L/cos β
N₁ = EAδ/L and N₂ = EAδ cos²β/L
N₁ = P/(1 + 2cos³β) and N₂ = P cos²β/(1 + 2cos³β)
The stiffer middle path carries the most load; as β → 90° the outer bars carry zero

boards.prompt: Contrast the force (flexibility) method with the displacement (stiffness) method for an indeterminate structure. When do you prefer each?
points: Force method unknowns are redundant forces; displacement method unknowns are joint displacements
Force method equations are compatibility; displacement method equations are equilibrium
Force method size equals the degree of indeterminacy; displacement method size equals the kinematic degrees of freedom
Both give the same unique answer for a linear structure
The displacement method is systematic and underlies finite elements; the force method suits hand problems with few redundants

boards.prompt: A long beam rests on an elastic (Winkler) foundation of modulus k and carries a point load P. Set it up and tell me how far the load is felt.
points: Governing equation: EI w⁗ + k w = q
Characteristic parameter β = (k/(4EI))^(1/4)
Solution decays as e^(−βx)(cos βx + sin βx) from the load
Peak deflection under the load: w = Pβ/(2k)
The load is felt over a length of order π/β, so a beam longer than that behaves as infinite

boards.prompt: A thick curved beam such as a crane hook is bent. Why does straight beam theory miss, where is the neutral axis, and where is the peak stress?
points: Inner fibres are shorter, so strain varies hyperbolically through the depth (Winkler)
The neutral axis shifts from the centroid toward the centre of curvature
Neutral axis radius r_n = A/∫(dA/r)
Rectangular section: r_n = h/ln(r_o/r_i)
Peak stress is at the inner fibre

boards.prompt: A portal frame has fixed bases, columns of height h and stiffness EI, and a rigid beam. Find the sway stiffness under a horizontal load at the top. Now pin the bases.
points: The rigid beam prevents rotation at the column tops
Both columns share the sway, so they act in parallel and stiffnesses add
Fixed base, guided top: each column gives 12EI/h³, total 24EI/h³
Pinned base, guided top: each column gives 3EI/h³, total 6EI/h³
Pinning the bases cuts the sway stiffness by a factor of four

boards.prompt: A steel bolt passes through an aluminium sleeve and the nut is turned until it advances by Δ. Find the preload. Then heat the assembly by ΔT.
points: Equilibrium: bolt tension equals sleeve compression, one force N
Compatibility: bolt stretch plus sleeve shortening equals the nut advance Δ
N = Δ/(L/(E_bA_b) + L/(E_sA_s)): the compliances add in series
Heating adds a free mismatch (α_s − α_b)ΔT L to the compatibility equation
Aluminium expands more than steel, so heating raises the preload

boards.prompt: Here is a three-hinged parabolic arch of span L and rise f under a uniform load per unit span. Find the support thrust and the bending moment in the arch.
points: Three hinges make the arch statically determinate
Vertical reactions wL/2 at each support
Moments about the crown hinge give horizontal thrust H = wL²/(8f)
The parabola matches the funicular shape, so the bending moment is zero everywhere
The arch carries the load in pure compression, and the thrust grows as the rise falls

boards.prompt: A pinned column carries an axial load P and a uniform lateral load. How does the midspan moment grow with P?
points: Beam-column equation: EI w⁗ + P w″ = q
The axial load acts on the lateral deflection, adding a P times δ moment
Moments and deflections are amplified by approximately 1/(1 − P/P_cr)
The amplification grows rapidly as P approaches P_cr
Superposition holds in q for a fixed P, while the response is nonlinear in P

boards.prompt: Restrain both ends of a pinned column with rotational springs C. How does P_cr move between the pinned and clamped limits?
points: End condition: the end moment EI w″ equals the spring moment C times the end slope
The symmetric mode gives tan(kL/2) = −kEI/C with k² = P/EI
C → 0 recovers π²EI/L², the pinned column
C → ∞ recovers 4π²EI/L², the clamped column
The effective length lies between L and L/2, governed by CL/EI

boards.prompt: Your column buckles above the proportional limit. Compare the tangent modulus and reduced modulus loads, and tell me which one you use.
points: Tangent modulus load: P_t = π²E_tI/L_e²
Reduced (double) modulus load uses E_r between E_t and E, so P_r ≥ P_t
Rectangle: E_r = 4EE_t/(√E + √E_t)²
Shanley showed bending starts at P_t under increasing load
Design uses the tangent modulus load as the practical critical load

boards.prompt: A thin-walled box column can buckle locally or as a whole. Give me both critical stresses and tell me how you design it.
points: Local plate buckling: σ_cr = kπ²E/(12(1 − ν²)) (t/b)²
k = 4 for a long plate with simply supported edges
Global Euler buckling: σ_cr = π²E/(L_e/r)²
Efficient design makes the local and global stresses close
Plates have stable post-buckling (effective width), so local buckling can be accepted below ultimate
